items.note: This is the only place where the two different definitions of RΓ_rig(X_0/r^†) — Grosse-Klönne's compactified deformation spaces and the naive one — have to be compared.

items.name: Theorem 4.12: the fundamental diagram for the pro-étale cohomology of a Stein semistable weak formal scheme
items.statement: Let X be a Stein semistable weak formal scheme over O_K and r ≥ 0. There is a natural map of strictly exact sequences of Fréchet spaces from 0 → Ω^{r−1}(X_C)/ker d → H^r_proét(X_C,Q_p(r)) → (H^r_HK(X_0) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{N=0,φ=p^r} → 0 to 0 → Ω^{r−1}(X_C)/ker d —d→ Ω^r(X_C)^{d=0} → H^r_dR(X_C) → 0, with the identity on the left, β̃ in the middle and ι_HK ⊗ θ on the right; the vertical maps have closed images and ker β̃ ≅ (H^r_HK(X_0) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{N=0,φ=p^{r−1}}. Here β̃ := p^{−r} β ι_rig^{−1} ι_BK^{−1} α_FM^{−1}, using Corollary 3.46, Proposition 3.48 and Theorem 4.1, the twist by p^{−r} being added to make the map compatible with symbols; the theorem then follows from Proposition 3.36.
items.note: This is Theorem 1.8, the main theorem of the paper, and the statement the companion papers cite for the closedness of the image in their fundamental diagram.

items.name: Remark 4.13: the comparison is one-way, and the contrast with the proper case
items.statement: Theorem 4.12 says that H^r_proét(X_C,Q_p(r)) is the pullback of (H^r_HK(X_0) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{N=0,φ=p^r} —ι_HK⊗θ→ H^r_dR(X_C) ←can— Ω^r(X_C)^{d=0}: it is built from Hyodo–Kato cohomology and a piece of the de Rham complex, with no converse recovering the Hyodo–Kato data. For X proper the semistable comparison theorem of Colmez–Nizioł gives instead 0 → H^r_proét(X_C,Q_p(r)) → (H^r_HK(X_0) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{N=0,φ=p^r} —ι_HK⊗ι→ (H^r_dR(X_K) ⊗̂_K B^+_dR)/F^r, i.e. the pullback along the zero map, étale and pro-étale cohomology agree, and the huge term disappears; the injectivity on the left comes from the degeneration of the Hodge–de Rham spectral sequence and the theory of finite dimensional Banach–Colmez spaces.
items.note: CP.4 owns the semistable B_st comparison for proper flat semistable models, which is exactly the statement (4.14) quoted here for contrast. As printed, the arrow in the second pullback description is labelled ι_HK ⊗ θ although its target is (H^r_dR ⊗̂ B^+_dR)/F^r; recorded in sourceIssues. Independent review: CP.4 supplies only the proper comparison part. The bundle also contains the nonproper Stein pullback and its topological comparison.
items.statusReview: CP.4 supplies only the proper comparison part. The bundle also contains the nonproper Stein pullback and its topological comparison.

items.name: Remark 4.15: the t-multiplication diagram relating the r- and (r−1)-twisted syntomic theories
items.statement: Writing HK^i_r, DR^i_r, Syn^i_r for the cohomology of HK(X_C,r), DR(X_C,r), RΓ_syn(X_C,Q_p(r)) and H^i_dR := H^i_dR(X_C), there is a commutative diagram with strictly exact rows — the long exact sequences for r−1 and for r, and the de Rham row — whose vertical maps from the first to the second row are multiplication by t ∈ (B^+_cr)^{φ=p} ∩ F^1B_dR (isomorphisms on the Syn-columns) and from the second to the third are θ, 0 or the identity according to the column, with short strictly exact columns. The columns are exact by the strictly exact sequences 0 → DR^i_{r−1} —t→ DR^i_r → H^i_dR(X_K) ⊗̂_K C → 0 (for r ≥ i+2, from 0 → gr^{r−i−1}_F B^+_dR ⊗̂_K (Ω^i(X_K)/dΩ^{i−1}(X_K)) → DR^i_r → (B^+_dR/F^{r−i−1}) ⊗̂_K H^i_dR(X_K) → 0) and 0 → HK^i_{r−1} —t→ HK^i_r → H^i_dR(X_K) ⊗̂_K C → 0 (from Lemma 3.39), together with the fact that multiplication by t identifies Syn^i_r with t·Syn^i_{r−1} for i ≤ r−1.
items.note: This is the structural explanation of why ker β̃ is the φ = p^{r−1} eigenspace: the two twists differ by multiplication by t.

items.name: Proposition 4.17: the pro-étale cohomology of rigid affine space, and the models used
items.statement: For r ≥ 1 there is a G_K-equivariant isomorphism of Fréchet spaces Ω^{r−1}(A^d_C)/ker d ≅→ H^r_proét(A^d_C,Q_p(r)), whereas H^r_ét(A^d_C,Q_p) = 0 for r ≥ 1 (Berkovich). The proof applies Theorem 4.12 to a semistable weak formal model: for d = 1 one takes the model of P_K ∖ L^* provided by Fresnel–van der Put's Theorem 4.9.1 with L = {∞} ∪ {ϖ^n : n ≤ 0} (the construction being easily modified to give a weak formal model), whose special fibre is a half line of projective lines; for d > 1 one takes the d-fold product over O^×_K of the logarithmic weak formal scheme attached to the d = 1 case, which is log-smooth but not semistable, and resolves it by blowing up the canonical ideal sheaf of Saito's Lemma 1.9. Since H^r_dR(A^d_K) = 0, the Hyodo–Kato isomorphism gives H^r_HK = 0 and the fundamental diagram collapses.
items.note: This is Example 1.9; simpler proofs are in Colmez–Nizioł (arXiv:1707.01133) and Le Bras. The existence of equivariant semistable models of rigid affine space and of the torus is itself a missing construction.

items.name: The fundamental diagram for the rigid torus
items.statement: For the d-dimensional rigid torus G^d_{m,K} there is a semistable weak formal model Y^d over O_K (for d = 1 from Fresnel–van der Put with L = {∞,0} ∪ {ϖ^n : n ∈ Z}, whose special fibre is a line of projective lines; for d > 1 by the same product-and-blow-up construction). Then H^r_dR(G^d_{m,K}) is a K-vector space of dimension C(d,r) generated by the products c^dR_1(z_{i_1})⋯c^dR_1(z_{i_r}) of de Rham Chern classes of the coordinates, H^r_HK(Y^d_0) is the analogous F-vector space generated by the c^HK_1(z_{i_j}), the two corresponding under ι_HK by Lemma 7.8, and since φ(c^HK_1(z)) = p·c^HK_1(z) and N(c^HK_1(z)) = 0 one gets (H^r_HK(Y^d_0) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{N=0,φ=p^r} = H^r_HK(Y^d_0)^{φ=p^r} = ∧^r Q_p^d. Theorem 4.12 then gives the map of G_K-equivariant exact sequences from 0 → Ω^{r−1}(G^d_{m,C})/ker d → H^r_proét(G^d_{m,C},Q_p(r)) → ∧^r Q_p^d → 0 to 0 → Ω^{r−1}(G^d_{m,C})/ker d —d→ Ω^r(G^d_{m,C})^{d=0} → ∧^r C^d → 0, with both vertical maps injective; for comparison H^r_ét(G^d_{m,C},Q_p(r)) ≅ ∧^r Q_p^d, generated by the étale symbols.
items.note: The cleanest illustration of what pro-étale cohomology adds to étale cohomology: the same finite-dimensional Q_p-space, extended by the huge Fréchet space of differential forms.

items.name: The fundamental diagram for a Stein curve
items.statement: For X a Stein curve over K with a semistable model X over O_K (the conditions of the model theorem are always satisfied for curves), Theorem 4.12 in degree r = 1 reads: a map from 0 → C^{π_0(X)} → O(X_C) —exp→ H^1_proét(X_C,Q_p(1)) → (H^1_HK(X_0) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{φ=p,N=0} → 0 to 0 → C^{π_0(X)} → O(X_C) —d→ Ω^1(X_C) → H^1_dR(X) ⊗̂_K C → 0, which is the identity on the first two terms, dlog in the middle and ι_HK ⊗ θ on the right.
items.note: This is the statement the companion paper PAPER-COLMEZ-DOSPINESCU-NIZIOL-20-B proves independently for curves (its Theorem 3.3) by the period-sheaf route, and which its extraction routed to ProetaleCohomologyOfPAdicCurvesAndTowers; here it is a corollary of the general theorem.

items.name: The standard G-equivariant semistable weak formal model of the Drinfeld half-space, and its special fibre
items.statement: H^d_K is a rigid analytic Stein space, hence also a dagger analytic Stein space, and it has a standard G-equivariant semistable weak formal model H̃^d_K over O_K, itself Stein, with generic fibre H^d_K (Grosse-Klönne). From §5.4.2 on one writes X := H̃^d_K and Y := H̃^d_{K,0} for its special fibre with the induced log structure. The set of K-rational hyperplanes is H := P((K^{d+1})^*) = P^d(K), a profinite set; for H ∈ H, ℓ_H ∈ (K^{d+1})^* is a (unimodular) linear equation of H.
items.note: This model is the X to which the comparison theorem (Theorem 4.12 = Theorem 1.8) is applied, and the object whose de Rham–Witt cohomology §6 computes. Nothing in the atlas constructs it.

items.name: The Bruhat–Tits building of PGL_{d+1}(K), its truncations BT_s, and the closed subschemes Y_s ⊂ Y
items.statement: The set of vertices of the Bruhat–Tits building BT of PGL_{d+1}(K) is the set of homothety classes [L] of lattices L ⊂ K^{d+1}, and it is in G-equivariant bijection with the set of irreducible components of Y = H̃^d_{K,0}. With base vertex v_0 = [O_K^{d+1}] and d(·,·) the combinatorial distance, BT_s is the simplicial subcomplex supported on the vertices v with d(v,v_0) ≤ s, and Y_s ⊂ Y is the union of the irreducible components corresponding to the vertices of BT_s, a closed subscheme with the induced log structure; Y_∞ = Y. One also sets Y_s^∘ := Y_s ∖ (Y_s ∩ closure(Y ∖ Y_s)), so that Y_{s−1} ⊂ Y_s^∘ ⊂ Y_s with the first immersion closed and the second open.
items.note: The exhaustion Y_s is what makes the Hyodo–Kato cohomology of Y a projective limit of finite-dimensional pieces ((5.12)), and it is the combinatorial backbone of the de Rham–Witt computation of §6. The atlas has Bruhat–Tits buildings only in the Tau Ceti reductive-groups roadmap (Layer 7) and in ReductiveGroupsPartII RG2.2/RG2.4; the identification of its vertices with the components of the special fibre of the standard model is specific to this geometry.

items.name: The Borel, the parabolics P_J and the profinite flag spaces X_J = G/P_J
items.statement: B ⊂ G = GL_{d+1}(K) is the upper triangular Borel and ∆ = {1,…,d}. The Weyl group W is the permutation group of {1,…,d+1}, generated by the transpositions s_i = (i,i+1), i ∈ ∆. For J ⊆ ∆, W_J ⊆ W is generated by the s_i with i ∈ J, P_J = B W_J B is the parabolic generated by B and W_J, and X_J := G/P_J is a compact profinite topological space; P_∅ = B, X_∆ is a point.
items.note: Standard parabolic subgroups of GL_{d+1} over a local field and their coset spaces; RG2.2 owns the valued/integral Bruhat–Tits and parabolic structure theory. Only the profinite topology and the LC-function spaces below are specific here. Independent review: Algebraic parabolics are supplied by upstream ReductiveGroups; RG2.0 supplies rational-point topologies and RG2.2 buildings. RG2.2 alone does not state this profinite flag quotient contract.
items.statusReview: Algebraic parabolics are supplied by upstream ReductiveGroups; RG2.0 supplies rational-point topologies and RG2.2 buildings. RG2.2 alone does not state this profinite flag quotient contract.

items.name: The generalized Steinberg representations Sp_J(A) and their degree-indexed form Sp_r(A)
items.statement: For an abelian group A and J ⊆ ∆, Sp_J(A) := LC(X_J, A) / Σ_{i ∈ ∆∖J} LC(X_{J∪{i}}, A), where LC(−,A) denotes locally constant A-valued functions (automatically compactly supported, the X_J being compact) and LC(X_{J∪{i}},A) is embedded by pullback along X_J → X_{J∪{i}}. It is a smooth Z[G]-module (an A[G]-module when A is a commutative ring), Sp_J(A) = Sp_J(Z) ⊗ A with Sp_J(Z) free, Sp_∅(A) is the usual Steinberg representation and Sp_∆(A) = A. One sets Sp_r(A) := Sp_{{1,…,d−r}}(A) for 0 ≤ r ≤ d and Sp_r(A) = 0 for r > d, so that Sp_0(A) = A and Sp_d(A) = Sp_∅(A).
items.note: The answer to every computation in the paper is a dual of one of these. The atlas mentions Steinberg representations only for GL_2 and in the automorphic/local-Langlands roadmaps (R16.3, R17.1, ET.6); the generalized Steinberg representations of GL_{d+1} over a local field, with the three topological flavours below, are not planned.

items.name: Proposition 5.1 (Casselman; Grosse-Klönne): the Sp_J are the irreducible constituents of LC(G/B,A)
items.statement: If A is a field of characteristic 0 or of characteristic p, then the Sp_J(A), for J ⊆ ∆, are exactly the irreducible constituents of the smooth G-module LC(G/B, A), each with multiplicity one.
items.note: Characteristic 0 is Casselman (Borel–Wallach X, Theorem 4.11); characteristic p is Grosse-Klönne [37, Cor. 4.3], and it is this mod p irreducibility that makes the étale computation work. Remark 5.2 records that the statement fails in characteristic ℓ ≠ p (Vignéras).

items.name: Corollary 5.3: Sp_J(O_K) is the unique G-stable lattice in Sp_J(K) up to homothety
items.statement: For J ⊆ ∆, Sp_J(O_K) is, up to a K^*-homothety, the unique G-stable O_K-lattice in Sp_J(K).
items.note: Proved from Proposition 5.1 and the finite generation of Sp_J(O_K) over O_K[G] (Grosse-Klönne [37, Cor. 4.5]). It is used in §6 (p. 52) to identify an integral lattice up to homothety, which is what lets the integral computation be pinned down.

items.name: The topologies on Sp_J(Λ) and on its dual: LF-spaces and nuclear Fréchet duals
items.statement: Let Λ be a topological ring. Writing the profinite X_J = lim←_n X_{n,J} with X_{n,J} finite gives LC(X_J,Λ) = lim→_n LC(X_{n,J},Λ) with each LC(X_{n,J},Λ) finite free over Λ, and hence a topology on Sp_J(Λ). For Λ a finite extension of Q_p this exhibits Sp_J(Λ) as an inductive limit of finite-dimensional Λ-vector spaces carrying the strongest locally convex topology, an LF-space. With M^* := Hom_cont(M,Λ) given the weak topology, Sp_J(Λ)^* is a countable inverse limit of finite free Λ-modules; so for L/Q_p finite, Sp_J(L)^* is a nuclear Fréchet space (in fact a countable product of Banach spaces), Sp_J(O_L)^* is a compact torsion-free O_L-module, and Sp_J(O_L)^* ⊗ L is the weak dual of an L-Banach space.
items.note: These topological facts are what make the answers of Theorems 1.3 and 5.13 Fréchet spaces and weak duals of Banach spaces. As printed, the displayed identification of the dual is of LC(X_J,Λ)^* rather than of the quotient Sp_J(Λ)^*; recorded in sourceIssues. Independent review: The exact dual description is the annihilator of the parabolic-function subspace inside LC(X_J,Λ)^*. Do not replace it by all distributions or assume arbitrary finite-level quotients are free; see E11.

items.name: The continuous generalized Steinberg representation Sp^cont_J(Λ) and its smooth vectors
items.statement: Sp^cont_J(Λ) := C(X_J,Λ) / Σ_{α ∈ ∆∖J} C(X_{J∪{α}},Λ) with C(−,Λ) the continuous Λ-valued functions. For L/Q_p finite, Sp^cont_J(L) is an L-Banach space with unit ball Sp^cont_J(O_L), G acts continuously, and Sp_J(L) is the subspace of smooth vectors of Sp^cont_J(L). One writes Sp^cont_r(Λ) := Sp^cont_{{1,…,d−r}}(Λ).
items.note: Sp^cont_r(Q_p)^* is the answer for étale cohomology (Theorem 1.3(1)), Sp_r(Q_p)^* for pro-étale cohomology (Theorem 1.3(2)); the whole point of part (3) is the passage between them.

items.name: Corollary 5.4: Sp^cont_J is the universal unitary completion, and its dual is the G-bounded part
items.statement: Let J ⊆ ∆ and let L be a finite extension of Q_p. (a) The universal unitary completion of Sp_J(L) is Sp^cont_J(L). (b) The space of G-bounded vectors in Sp_J(L)^* is Sp^cont_J(L)^*.
items.note: (a) follows from Corollary 5.3 and the fact that Sp^cont_J(O_L) is the p-adic completion of Sp_J(O_L); (b) follows from (a) by duality. This is the representation-theoretic half of Theorem 1.3(3): the G-bounded vectors of the pro-étale answer are the étale answer.

items.name: Remark 5.5: the locally analytic generalized Steinberg representation Sp^an_J(L)
items.statement: For L a finite extension of Q_p (or any closed subfield of C) there is a locally analytic generalized Steinberg representation Sp^an_J(L): a space of compact type whose dual is a nuclear Fréchet space, containing Sp_J(L) as a closed subspace — closed because Sp_J(L) is exactly the subspace of vectors killed by the Lie algebra of G. Dually, Sp^an_J(L)^* surjects onto Sp_J(L)^* and contains Sp^cont_J(L)^* as a dense subspace. Unlike Sp_J(L) and Sp^cont_J(L), Sp^an_J(L) is topologically reducible as a G-module; its Jordan–Hölder constituents are described by Orlik–Schraen.
items.note: The locally analytic side belongs to the roadmap proposed by PAPER-DING-25 (locally analytic representations of p-adic reductive groups, with the Orlik–Strauch functors); the Jordan–Hölder series of the locally analytic Steinberg representation is exactly the Orlik–Schraen theorem that roadmap should carry.

items.name: Simplicial profinite flag objects and the normalized semisimplicial strict flags
items.statement: Fix r ∈ {1,…,d}. Y^{(r)}_s is the closed subset of H^{s+1} of tuples (H_0,…,H_s) with dim_K(Σ_i K·ℓ_{H_i}) ≤ r. T^{(r)}_s is the profinite set of (not necessarily strict) flags W_0 ⊆ … ⊆ W_s of subspaces of (K^{d+1})^* with dim W_i ∈ {1,…,r}, and N T^{(r)}_s ⊆ T^{(r)}_s the clopen subset of strict flags; the ambient face and degeneracy maps (on N T only the face maps restrict) omit or repeat a hyperplane resp. a subspace, G-equivariantly. Forgetting the topology, T^{(d)}_• is the Tits building of G (not the Bruhat–Tits building). The cohomology used here is computed with locally constant cochains and alternating face differentials; the comparison of these particular flag objects is supplied by Schneider–Stuhler. No unrestricted identification with singular cohomology of every underlying simplicial set is asserted. There are G-equivariant identifications N T^{(r)}_{r−1} ≅ X_{{1,…,d−r}} and N T^{(r)}_{r−2} ≅ ⊔_{i=d−r+1}^{d} X_{{1,…,d−r,i}}.
items.note: This is the combinatorial engine of Schneider–Stuhler: the identifications with flag spaces are exactly the numerator and denominator of the definition of Sp_r, which is why the cohomology of the building computes the Steinberg representation. Independent review: The nondegenerate strict-flag object N T is semisimplicial: face maps preserve strictness, degeneracies do not. Degeneracy operators belong to the ambient simplicial flag object, not its normalized strict flags.

items.name: Proposition 5.6 and Remark 5.7: the cohomology of the Tits-type complexes is Sp_r(Z)
items.statement: For all r ∈ {1,…,d} there are natural G-equivariant isomorphisms of reduced cohomology H̃^{r−1}(|T^{(r)}_•|,Z) ≅ H̃^{r−1}(|Y^{(r)}_•|,Z) ≅ Sp_r(Z). Moreover, for all q there are natural isomorphisms H^q(|N T^{(r)}_•|,Z) ≅ H^q(|T^{(r)}_•|,Z) ≅ H^q(|Y^{(r)}_•|,Z), and these groups vanish except for q = 0 and q = r − 1, the degree-0 group being Z for r > 1 and LC(P((K^{d+1})^*),Z) for r = 1.
items.note: Proved from Schneider–Stuhler [73, Ch. 3, Props 5 and 6] together with the flag-space identifications. The concentration in degrees 0 and r−1 is what collapses the support spectral sequence in the proof of Theorem 5.8.

items.name: Theorem 5.8 (Schneider–Stuhler): the ℓ-adic and de Rham cohomology of the Drinfeld half-space
items.statement: Let r ≥ 0. (a) For a prime ℓ ≠ p there are natural isomorphisms of G × G_K-modules H^r_ét(H^d_C, Q_ℓ(r)) ≅ Sp_r(Z_ℓ)^* ⊗ Q_ℓ and H^r_proét(H^d_C, Q_ℓ(r)) ≅ Sp_r(Q_ℓ)^*. (b) There is a natural isomorphism of G-modules H^r_dR(H^d_K) ≅ Sp_r(K)^*.
items.note: One of the main results of Schneider–Stuhler; Orlik gives a different argument for the de Rham statement and its compactly supported analogue. The proof uses the Stein exhaustion U_n = ∩_{H} U_n(H), the spectral sequence with supports and homotopy invariance for the disc — the axiom that fails for p-adic étale cohomology.

items.name: The Stein exhaustion U_n of the half-space and the support spectral sequence
items.statement: For H ∈ H and n ≥ 1, U_n(H) is the open polydisc in the affine space P^d_K ∖ H defined by |ℓ_H(z)| > |ϖ|^n (unimodular representatives being used for points and linear forms). The U_n := ∩_{H ∈ H} U_n(H) form a Stein covering of H^d_K, and U_n = ∩_{H ∈ H_n} U_n(H) for a finite subset H_n ⊆ H in bijection with P^d((O_K^{d+1}/ϖ^n)^*). Writing H^*(X,U) for cohomology with support in X ∖ U (the derived functors of sections vanishing on U), there is a spectral sequence E_1^{−j,i}(n) = ⊕_{H_0,…,H_j ∈ H_n} H^i(P^d_K, U_n(H_0) ∪ … ∪ U_n(H_j)) ⇒ H^{i−j}(P^d_K, U_n); each union is a locally trivial fibration over a projective space with open polydisc fibres, so homotopy invariance makes each E_1-term either the coefficient ring or 0 by a combinatorial recipe, and passing to the limit over n and using Proposition 5.6 and Remark 5.7 gives a spectral sequence converging to H^{i−j}(P^d_K, H^d_K), which the long exact sequence of the pair converts into H^*(H^d_K).
items.note: The exhaustion U_n is reused for the regulators (the symbol map is locally constant on each U_n, not on the whole space) and in §6. Note the two printed occurrences of an undefined uniformiser π here, recorded in sourceIssues.

items.name: Corollary 5.9: the G-bounded vectors of the de Rham cohomology of the half-space
items.statement: The space of G-bounded vectors in H^r_dR(H^d_K) ≅ Sp_r(K)^* is isomorphic to Sp^cont_r(K)^*.
items.note: Theorem 5.8 combined with Corollary 5.4(b). Used in §6 (p. 52) to identify the integral image with Sp^cont_r(O_F)^* ⊗_{O_F} F, and in the proof of Theorem 1.3(3).

items.name: The cocycle space LC_c(H^{r+1},Z) and the identification Sp_r(Z) ≅ LC_c(H^{r+1},Z)
items.statement: LC_c(H^{r+1},Z) is the space of locally constant f : H^{r+1} → Z such that (i) for all H_0,…,H_{r+1} ∈ H the alternating sum f(H_1,…,H_{r+1}) − f(H_0,H_2,…,H_{r+1}) + … + (−1)^{r+1} f(H_0,…,H_r) vanishes, and (ii) f(H_0,…,H_r) = 0 whenever the ℓ_{H_i} are linearly dependent, i.e. f vanishes on Y^{(r)}_r. There are natural G-equivariant isomorphisms H̃^{r−1}(|N T^{(r)}_•|,Z) ≅ LC_c(H^{r+1},Z) and hence Sp_r(Z) ≅ LC_c(H^{r+1},Z).
items.note: This explicit cocycle model of the Steinberg representation is what turns the abstract isomorphisms of Theorem 5.8 into statements about symbols, and it is what the Hyodo–Kato computation of Lemma 5.11 exploits.

items.name: Distributions and measures on H^{r+1}, the hyperplane symbols, and the regulator maps
items.statement: For a profinite set S and an abelian group A, D(S,A) := Hom(LC(S,Z),A) is the space of A-valued locally constant distributions; for a discretely valued nonarchimedean field L, M(S,L) is the space of L-valued measures (bounded distributions), whose natural topology is finer than the one induced from D(S,L). The inclusion LC_c(H^{r+1},Z) ⊂ LC(H^{r+1},Z) induces a continuous strict surjection D(H^{r+1},A) → Hom(Sp_r(Z),A), whose kernel is by definition the space D(H^{r+1},A)_deg of degenerate distributions; combined with Theorem 5.8 this gives surjections D(H^{r+1},K) → H^r_dR(H^d_K), M(H^{r+1},Q_ℓ) → H^r_ét(H^d_C,Q_ℓ(r)) and D(H^{r+1},Q_ℓ) → H^r_proét(H^d_C,Q_ℓ(r)). For (H_0,…,H_r) ∈ H^{r+1} the functions ℓ_{H_1}/ℓ_{H_0}, …, ℓ_{H_r}/ℓ_{H_0} are invertible on H^d_K, and taking dlog and wedge products (or étale symbols and cup products) gives the symbol [H_0,…,H_r] — in de Rham cohomology the class of the closed r-form dlog(ℓ_{H_1}/ℓ_{H_0}) ∧ … ∧ dlog(ℓ_{H_r}/ℓ_{H_0}). The regulators r_dR(μ) = ∫_{H^{r+1}} [H_0,…,H_r] μ(H_0,…,H_r), and likewise r_ét and r_proét, are well defined and continuous: the symbol map is not locally constant into the cohomology of H^d_K but is so after restriction to each U_n, and in the pro-étale case one uses H^r_proét(H^d_C,Q_ℓ(r)) = lim←_n H^r_proét(U_{n,C},Q_ℓ(r)) with finite-dimensional terms.
items.note: The symbols are the bridge between the three cohomologies: it is because de Rham cohomology and the Steinberg dual are both generated by the standard symbols, compatibly, that the Hyodo–Kato cohomology can be identified in Lemma 5.11. The atlas plans symbols only in K-theoretic form (K2SymbolsBrauer T.1/T.2) and p-adic regulators in PadicHodgeRegulators D.2/D.5, neither of which covers distribution-valued regulators on a symmetric space.

items.name: Theorem 5.10 (Iovita–Spiess): the regulator sequence is strictly exact and computes the de Rham cohomology
items.statement: The diagram of Fréchet G-spaces formed by the strictly exact sequence 0 → D(H^{r+1},K)_deg → D(H^{r+1},K) —r_dR→ H^r_dR(H^d_K) → 0, the canonical strict surjection D(H^{r+1},K) ↠ Sp_r(K)^* and the isomorphism Sp_r(K)^* ≅ H^r_dR(H^d_K) of Theorem 5.8(b), commutes; i.e. the regulator r_dR is identified with the canonical surjection. The same holds for ℓ-adic étale cohomology with M(H^{r+1},Q_ℓ) and for pro-étale cohomology with D(H^{r+1},Q_ℓ).
items.note: This is the statement the introduction quotes as "Iovita–Spiess prove that H^r_dR(X_K) is generated by standard symbols, compatibly with the isomorphism". Lemma 5.11 is its Hyodo–Kato generalisation.

items.name: Lemma 5.11: the Hyodo–Kato cohomology of the Drinfeld half-space is a Steinberg dual
items.statement: Let r ≥ 0, X = H̃^d_K and Y = H̃^d_{K,0}. There are natural isomorphisms of Fréchet spaces H^r_HK(Y) ≅ Sp_r(F)^* and H^r_HK(Y)^{φ=p^r} ≅ Sp_r(Q_p)^*, compatible with the isomorphism H^r_dR(X_K) ≅ Sp_r(K)^* of Theorem 5.8 through ι_HK and with the base-change maps Sp_r(Q_p)^* → Sp_r(F)^* → Sp_r(K)^*.
items.note: The proof defines a Hyodo–Kato regulator r_HK : D(H^{r+1},F) → H^r_HK(Y) by integrating the overconvergent Hyodo–Kato symbols of §7.2.1, uses Lemma 7.8 (ι_HK is compatible with the Chern classes) and Theorem 5.10 to get a continuous f : Sp_r(F)^* → H^r_HK(Y), and proves it bijective using the topological irreducibility of H^r_HK(Y) as a G-module and the closedness of Sp_r(F)^* in Sp_r(K)^*. The φ = p^r statement uses that r_HK restricted to D(H^{r+1},Q_p) factors through the φ = p^r part.

items.name: Equation (5.12): the φ = p^r part of Hyodo–Kato cohomology injects after base change to F
items.statement: The natural map H^r_HK(Y)^{φ=p^r} ⊗_{Q_p} F → H^r_HK(Y) is injective. This follows from H^r_HK(Y) ≅ lim←_s H^r_HK(Y_s), the commutation of the φ = p^r part with the limit and with ⊗_{Q_p} F, and the finite dimensionality of each H^r_HK(Y_s) over F.
items.note: This is where the exhaustion Y_s of the special fibre is used; it gives the surjectivity half of Lemma 5.11 and the second isomorphism of the chain in §5.5. Independent review: Commutation of scalar extension with the displayed inverse limit uses F/Q_p finite, not just finite dimensionality of each individual term.

items.name: Frobenius acts by q^r and the monodromy vanishes on the Hyodo–Kato cohomology of the half-space
items.statement: For r ≥ 0 the linearised Frobenius on H^r_HK(Y) is multiplication by q^r, where q = |k| (Grosse-Klönne [32, Cor. 6.6]); since Nφ = pφN ([32, Prop. 5.5]) the monodromy operator N is trivial on H^r_HK(Y). Consequently (H^r_HK(Y) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{N=0,φ=p^r} ≅ (H^r_HK(Y) ⊗̂_F B^+_cr)^{φ=p^r}, Galois-equivariantly.
items.note: This is why no monodromy term appears in Theorem 5.13, and why the answer for the half-space is so much simpler than for the Drinfeld tower, where N is non-trivial.

items.name: The computation (H^r_HK(Y) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{N=0,φ=p^r} ≅ Sp_r(Q_p)^*, and the vanishing of the φ = p^{r−1} part
items.statement: One has (H^r_HK(Y) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{N=0,φ=p^r} ≅ (H^r_HK(Y) ⊗̂_F B^+_cr)^{φ=p^r} ≅ (H^r_HK(Y)^{φ=p^r} ⊗̂_{Q_p} B^+_cr)^{φ=p^r} ≅ H^r_HK(Y)^{φ=p^r} ⊗̂_{Q_p} (B^+_cr)^{φ=1} ≅ Sp_r(Q_p)^* ⊗̂_{Q_p} (B^+_cr)^{φ=1} = Sp_r(Q_p)^*, using N = 0, (5.12), Lemma 5.11 and (B^+_cr)^{φ=1} = Q_p; under these identifications the map ι_HK ⊗ θ of Theorem 4.12 becomes the canonical map Sp_r(Q_p)^* → Sp_r(K)^* ⊗̂_K C. Similarly (H^r_HK(Y) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{N=0,φ=p^{r−1}} ≅ H^r_HK(Y)^{φ=p^r} ⊗̂_{Q_p} (B^+_cr)^{φ=p^{−1}} = 0, so by Theorem 4.12 the map β̃ is injective with closed image.
items.note: The vanishing of (B^+_cr)^{φ=p^{−1}} is what makes the pro-étale cohomology of the half-space an extension rather than a more complicated pullback; for the Drinfeld tower the corresponding term does not vanish.

items.name: Theorem 5.13: the p-adic pro-étale cohomology of the Drinfeld half-space
items.statement: Let r ≥ 0. There is a natural map of strictly exact sequences of G × G_K-Fréchet spaces over Q_p from 0 → Ω^{r−1}(H^d_C)/ker d → H^r_proét(H^d_C, Q_p(r)) → Sp_r(Q_p)^* → 0 to 0 → Ω^{r−1}(H^d_C)/ker d —d→ Ω^r(H^d_C)^{d=0} → Sp_r(K)^* ⊗̂_K C → 0, which is the identity on the left, β̃ in the middle and the canonical map Sp_r(Q_p)^* → Sp_r(K)^* ⊗̂_K C on the right; the vertical maps are closed immersions. Equivalently, H^r_proét(H^d_C,Q_p(r)) is the pullback of Ω^r(H^d_C)^{d=0} → Sp_r(K)^* ⊗̂_K C ← Sp_r(Q_p)^*. Since Sp_r = 0 for r > d, the sequences degenerate outside 1 ≤ r ≤ d.
items.note: This is Theorem 1.3(2) and the pro-étale half of the main theorem: the answer is the ℓ-adic Steinberg dual extended by the huge Fréchet space Ω^{r−1}/ker d.

items.name: Proposition 6.1: the integral Fontaine–Messing period map and its p^N-inverse
items.statement: Let X be a semistable formal scheme over O_K, r≥0 and X̄=X_{O_C}. The Fontaine–Messing map α_FM:RΓ_syn(X̄,Z_p(r))⊗^LQ_p → RΓ_ét(X_C,Z_p(r))⊗^LQ_p is a strict quasi-isomorphism in D(C_{Q_p}) after τ^{≤r}. On a finite-type semistable piece Y, the integral map α̃_FM:RΓ_syn(Y_{O_C},Z_p(r)) → RΓ_ét(Y_C,Z_p(r)′) has kernel and cokernel killed by a universal p^{N(r)} in degrees 0 through r. The modified lattice Z_p(r)′ must be taken with the Fontaine–Messing normalization; the inclusive remainder interval printed here is ambiguous (E30) and is a supplier-normalization obligation. Apply the cone bound to the truncated map, enlarging the exponent if necessary. Define the global map by cohomological descent on quasi-compact étale hypercovers, and α_FM=p^{−r}(α̃_FM⊗^LQ_p), with the indicated symbol normalization. In the bounded derived category a p^M-inverse exists for a possibly enlarged M=M(r), hence the rationalized map is invertible. Remark 6.2 supplies the pro-discrete topology; neither the untruncated integral map nor the same numerical exponent in every step is asserted.
items.note: This is the étale half of Proposition 1.11. The p^N-inverse device is reused in Lemma 6.34. Note that the integral theory lives in pro-discrete modules (§2.2), and the topology on both sides is that of §2.2 (Remark 6.2): locally complexes of topologically free Z_p-modules with the p-adic topology, globally the total complex of a Čech complex, so each degree is a product. Independent review: A p-power inverse in the bounded derived category may require enlarging the exponent. As p. 44 explicitly says, it need not be the same N; only the dependence N=N(r) is retained. The modified Tate lattice needs an unambiguous quotient–remainder convention (E30).

items.name: The standard formal model of the half-space, its components, the central component T and the divisors V
items.statement: Write X̃ = H̃^d_K for the standard weak formal model and X for its p-adic completion, both G-equivariant, with Y := X_0 and Ȳ := Y_{k̄}. F^0 is the set of irreducible components of Y; they are pairwise isomorphic smooth projective k-schemes, viewed as log schemes with the log structure induced from Y. T is the central component, the one with stabiliser K^* GL_{d+1}(O_K); it is obtained from P^d_k by blowing up all k-rational points, then the strict transforms of the k-rational lines, and so on. For 0 ≤ j ≤ d−1, V^j_0 is the set of k-rational linear subvarieties of P^d_k of dimension j, V_0 their union, and V the set of strict transforms in T of the elements of V_0 — a set of divisors which, with the canonical log structure of the log point k^0, induces the log structure of T. The truncations Y_s and the opens Y_s^∘ are those of §5.1, ideally log-smooth and proper over k^0 but not log-smooth. θ_0,…,θ_d denote the standard projective coordinates on P^d_k and on T, and the forms g·dlog(θ_i/θ_j) for g ∈ G, together with their exterior products, are the standard logarithmic differential forms on T.
items.note: The explicit blow-up description of T is what makes its strata products of blow-ups of projective spaces, hence classically ordinary, which is the geometric input behind pro-ordinarity.

items.name: Propositions 6.3–6.7: acyclicity of the sheaves of differentials and the vanishing of d on global sections
items.statement: Grosse-Klönne's computations give: (Proposition 6.3) H^i(T,Ω^j) = 0 for i > 0 and j ≥ 0; H^0(T,Ω^j) is generated by standard logarithmic forms, hence killed by d; and H^i_cr(T/O^0_F) is torsion free with H^i_cr(T/O^0_F) ⊗_{O_F} k = H^i_dR(T) = H^0(T,Ω^i_T). (Proposition 6.4) The canonical maps L^{j,0}_T ↪ L^j_T ↪ Ω^j_T and L^j_E ↪ Ω^j_T ⊗ O_E induce isomorphisms on Zariski cohomology, where L^j_T ⊂ Ω^j_T(T^0), T^0 = T ∖ ∪_{V ∈ V} V, is spanned by the forms y_1^{m_1}⋯y_j^{m_j} dlog y_1 ∧ ⋯ ∧ dlog y_j with y_i = θ_i/θ_0 in suitable coordinates. (Proposition 6.5) H^i(X,Ω^j_X) = 0 and H^i(X,Ω^j_X ⊗_{O_K} k) = 0 for i > 0, H^0(X,Ω^j_X) ⊗_{O_K} k ≅ H^0(X,Ω^j_X ⊗_{O_K} k), and d = 0 on H^0(X,Ω^j_X); hence (Corollary 6.6) H^0(X,Ω^j_X) ≅ H^j_dR(X), torsion free. (Proposition 6.7) H^i(Y_s,Ω^j) = 0 for i > 0 and d = 0 on H^0(Y_s,Ω^j), proved from a Mayer–Vietoris sequence over the simplices of BT_s together with an acyclicity criterion for coefficient systems on the truncated building (Lemma 6.8): if for every pointed (r−1)-simplex η̂ and every stable subset M_0 ⊆ N_η̂ the subquotient complex F(η) → ∏_{z ∈ M_0} F({z}∪η) → ∏_{z,z′} F({z,z′}∪η) is exact, then H^r(BT_s,F) = 0.
items.note: All the acyclicity input is Grosse-Klönne's; the extension of his building criterion from BT to the truncations BT_s is done here. Nothing in the atlas computes cohomology of coefficient systems on a Bruhat–Tits building.

items.name: Ordinarity of log schemes: the criteria of Lorenzon and Illusie, and the criterion from acyclicity
items.statement: For V a fine (idealized) log scheme over k^0 of Cartier type let B^j_V := im(d : Ω^{j−1} → Ω^j) and Z^j_V := ker(d : Ω^j → Ω^{j+1}); for V proper and log-smooth, V is ordinary if H^i_ét(V,B^j) = 0 for all i,j ≥ 0. Proposition 6.9 (Lorenzon): for V proper log-smooth the following are equivalent — V is ordinary; H^i_ét(V̄,Ω^j_log) ⊗_{F_p} k̄ ≅ H^i_ét(V̄,Ω^j) for all i,j; the canonical maps H^i_ét(V̄,W_nΩ^j_log) ⊗_{Z/p^n} W_n(k̄) → H^i_ét(V̄,W_nΩ^j) and H^i_ét(V̄,WΩ^j_log) ⊗_{Z_p} W(k̄) → H^i_ét(V̄,WΩ^j) are isomorphisms; the de Rham–Witt Frobenius F is an isomorphism on H^i_ét(V̄,WΩ^j). Projective spaces are ordinary, and projective bundles over an ordinary base are ordinary. For a smooth closed centre Y of codimension at least two in proper smooth X, the usual blow-up criterion says X and Y are ordinary if and only if Bl_Y(X) is; the paper omits that codimension qualification (source issue E32). For a Cartier divisor Bl_Y(X)=X, so its ordinarity cannot detect that of Y, and a semistable k̄-scheme all of whose strata are smooth and ordinary is ordinary as a log scheme over k^0, by the weight spectral sequence and the Frobenius-equivariance of its E_1-term. Lemma 6.13: if V is a fine (idealized) log scheme of Cartier type over k^0 with H^i_ét(V,Ω^j) = 0 for i ≥ 1 and d = 0 on H^0_ét(V,Ω^j), then V is ordinary, by induction on j along the two exact sequences 0 → B^j → Z^j → Ω^j → 0 and 0 → Z^j → Ω^j → B^{j+1} → 0 and the Cartier isomorphism C : Z^j/B^j ≅ Ω^j.
items.note: CR.4 is titled "Ordinary and relative de Rham–Witt complexes" and constructs W_nΩ with F, V, Teichmüller lifts and dlog; the logarithmic de Rham–Witt sheaves WΩ^j_log, the notion of an ordinary log scheme and the equivalent criteria of Bloch–Kato, Illusie–Raynaud and Lorenzon are not planned there, and the paper is a consumer of the former and a source for the latter. Independent review: Ordinary in the title of CR.4 distinguishes classical de Rham–Witt from relative theory; that stage does not state the ordinarity criteria for log schemes, the blow-up criterion or the acyclicity argument.
items.statusReview: Ordinary in the title of CR.4 distinguishes classical de Rham–Witt from relative theory; that stage does not state the ordinarity criteria for log schemes, the blow-up criterion or the acyclicity argument.

items.name: Corollary 6.18 and Remark 6.19: the special fibre of the standard model is pro-ordinary
items.statement: The idealized log schemes Y_s, s ∈ N ∪ {∞}, are ordinary, i.e. H^i_ét(Y_s,B^j) = 0 for all i,j ≥ 0: for s < ∞ this follows from Lemma 6.13 and Proposition 6.7, and for s = ∞ (that is, for Y and Ȳ) from Proposition 6.5 together with the limit argument inside the proof of Lemma 6.20. Remark 6.19 notes that the underlying scheme of Y_s, s < ∞, is classically ordinary by the weight spectral sequence, its strata being iterated blow-ups of projective spaces, and that Corollary 6.18 should be provable the same way.
items.note: This is the "X_k̄ is pro-ordinary" of the introduction. The term pro-ordinary is used in the subsection title and the introduction but never defined; it means that the special fibre is the increasing union of the ordinary truncations Y_s.

items.name: Lemma 6.20: vanishing of the higher cohomology of W_nΩ^j and strict exactness of the Verschiebung sequence
items.statement: For i ≥ 1 and j ≥ 0: H^i_ét(Z,W_nΩ^j) = 0 for Z = Y and Z = T; d = 0 on H^0_ét(T,W_nΩ^j); and for V = Y and V = Ȳ the sequence 0 → H^0(V,Ω^j) —V^n→ H^0(V,W_{n+1}Ω^j) → H^0(V,W_nΩ^j) → 0 is strictly exact. The proof uses the filtration 0 = B^j_0 ⊂ B^j_1 ⊂ … ⊂ Z^j_1 ⊂ Z^j_0 = Ω^j with the inverse Cartier isomorphisms B^j_n ≅ B^j_{n+1}/B^j_1 and Z^j_n ≅ Z^j_{n+1}/B^j_1, the vanishing H^i(Y,B^j_1) = H^i(Y,Z^j_1) = 0 for i > 0 from Proposition 6.5 and Lemma 6.13, the auxiliary sheaf R^j_n defined by 0 → R^j_n → B^j_{n+1} ⊕ Z^{j−1}_n → B^j_1 → 0, and the Hyodo–Kato exact sequence 0 → (Ω^j ⊕ Ω^{j−1})/R^j_n → W_{n+1}Ω^j → W_nΩ^j → 0, together with ordinarity of T_{k̄} for the vanishing of d.
items.note: This is the acyclicity of the de Rham–Witt sheaves that the introduction calls the second pillar of the étale computation; the surjectivity in the Verschiebung sequence is what gives the Mittag-Leffler property used at every limit.

items.name: Proposition 6.23: acyclicity and base change with orthonormalisable topological coefficients
items.statement: Let j ≥ 0, let S be a topologically orthonormalisable topological O_K-module and R a topologically orthonormalisable topological W(k)- or W(k̄)-module. Then the natural maps H^0(X,Ω^j_{X,n}) ⊗̂_{O_{K,n}} S_n → RΓ(X,Ω^j_{X,n}) ⊗̂_{O_{K,n}} S_n, H^0_ét(Y,W_nΩ^j) ⊗̂_{O_{F,n}} R_n → RΓ_ét(Y,W_nΩ^j) ⊗̂_{O_{F,n}} R_n, RΓ_ét(Ȳ,W_nΩ^j_log) ⊗̂_{Z/p^n} R_n → RΓ_ét(Ȳ,W_nΩ^j) ⊗̂_{W_n(k̄)} R_n and H^0_ét(Ȳ,W_nΩ^j_log) ⊗̂_{Z/p^n} R_n → RΓ_ét(Ȳ,W_nΩ^j_log) ⊗̂_{Z/p^n} R_n are strict quasi-isomorphisms; d = 0 on H^0(X,Ω^j_{X,n}) ⊗̂ S_n and on H^0_ét(Ȳ,W_nΩ^j) ⊗̂ R_n; and ⊕_{j ≥ r} H^0(X,Ω^j_{X,n})[−j] → F^r RΓ_dR(X_n) is a strict quasi-isomorphism. The proof degenerates the spectral sequence of the exhaustion, using that the pro-systems over the Y_s^∘ and the Y_s are equivalent with H̃^i(Y_s,Ω^j_n) classical of finite type, and embeds the limit into a product over an orthonormal basis of S_n.
items.note: The finite-level vanishing and the change of coefficient base must be separated. The printed Z/p^n tensor in part (2) is not a false statement: its cohomology factor is zero. The geometric base-change part needs a W(k̄)-algebra R.

items.name: Corollary 6.25: the logarithmic de Rham–Witt cohomology of the standard model
items.statement: For j ≥ 0 there is a canonical topological isomorphism H^0_ét(Ȳ,Ω^j_log) ⊗̂_{F_p} k̄ ≅ H^0_ét(Ȳ,Ω^j); for j,n ≥ 0 the canonical maps H^0_ét(Ȳ,W_nΩ^j_log) ⊗̂_{Z/p^n} W_n(k̄) → H^0_ét(Ȳ,W_nΩ^j) and H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^j_log) ⊗̂_{Z_p} W(k̄) → H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^j) are topological isomorphisms, and in higher degrees all these groups vanish; and H̃^i(X,Ω^j_X) and H̃^j_dR(X) are classical with H^i(X,Ω^j_X) = 0 for i > 0 and H^j_dR(X) ≅ H^0(X,Ω^j_X). The p-adic statements follow by Mittag-Leffler from the finite-level ones, using Lemma 6.20.
items.note: This is (1.14) of the introduction, the statement that the logarithmic de Rham–Witt cohomology of the special fibre computes the crystalline cohomology; Appendix A gives a second proof of it that avoids the ordinarity of the truncations Y_s.

items.name: Proposition 6.27: injectivity of the de Rham–Witt-to-rigid and of the model-to-generic-fibre maps
items.statement: For the standard model X of H^d_K, with Y=X_0 over the finite residue field k, define ι_Y as H^i_ét(Y,WΩ^•) ≅ H^i_cr(Y/O_F^0) → H^i_cr(Y/O_F^0,F) ←≅ H^i_rig(Y/O_F^0) → H^i_rig(Y/O_K^×), the last map induced by Hyodo–Kato. Proposition 6.27(1) states that the induced map H^i_ét(Y,WΩ^•) ⊗_{O_F} F → H^i_rig(Y/O_K^×) is injective. Part (2) states that H^i_dR(X) ⊗_{O_K} K → H^i_dR(X_K) is injective. The proof restricts to the product of the irreducible components C_j of Y, uses H^0_ét(Z,WΩ^i) ≅ H^i_ét(Z,WΩ^•) for Z=Y and C_j, torsion-freeness and injectivity of restriction to the nonsingular locus, then uses the bounded Hyodo–Kato comparison of §7. The first tensor is with F, exactly as printed on p. 51; it is not the extraction’s stronger K-linearized assertion.
items.note: The injectivity of H^i_dR(X) ⊗ K → H^i_dR(X_K) — that the bounded de Rham cohomology of the model injects into that of the generic fibre — is what makes the integral computation detect the rational one, and it is used again in Corollary 6.42 and Theorem 6.45(4).

items.name: Theorem 6.28: the de Rham–Witt and de Rham cohomology of the model are duals of continuous Steinberg representations
items.statement: Let K/Q_p be finite, X the standard formal model of H^d_K, Y=X_0 and Ȳ=Y_{k̄}. For r≥0, Theorem 6.28 gives topological isomorphisms (1a) H^0_ét(Y,WΩ^r)⊗_{O_F}F ≅ H^r_ét(Y,WΩ^•)⊗_{O_F}F ≅ Sp^cont_r(F)^*; (1b) H^0_ét(Y,WΩ^r_log)⊗Q_p ≅ Sp^cont_r(Q_p)^*; (1c) H^0(X,Ω^r)⊗_{O_K}K ≅ H^r_dR(X)⊗_{O_K}K ≅ Sp^cont_r(K)^*; (1d) H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^r_log)⊗Q_p ≅ Sp^cont_r(Q_p)^*. Integrally, (2a) H^0_ét(Y,WΩ^r) ≅ H^r_ét(Y,WΩ^•) ≅ Sp^cont_r(O_F)^* and H^0_ét(Y,Ω^r) ≅ Sp_r(k)^*; (2b) H^0_ét(Y,WΩ^r_log) ≅ Sp^cont_r(Z_p)^* and H^0_ét(Y,Ω^r_log) ≅ Sp_r(F_p)^*; (2c) H^0(X,Ω^r) ≅ H^r_dR(X) ≅ Sp^cont_r(O_K)^*; (2d) the same logarithmic identifications hold with Ȳ in place of Y. These are isomorphisms of pro-discrete Z_p-modules in (2) and weak duals of Banach spaces in (1), compatible with scalar extension and the maps to H^r_dR(X_K)≅Sp_r(K)^* and H^r_HK(Y)≅Sp_r(F)^*. The preceding vanishing results distinguish ordinary Witt forms on Y from their W(k̄)-base changes on Ȳ.
items.note: These refinements of Schneider–Stuhler, Iovita–Spiess and Grosse-Klönne are what Remark 1.5 refers to. The proof runs through the three regulator diagrams below and uses the uniqueness of the G-stable lattice (Corollary 5.3) and the mod p irreducibility of the Steinberg representation.

items.name: The integral regulators r_HK, r_log and r_dR and the three diagrams that identify them
items.statement: For K/Q_p finite and the standard model X with Y=X_0, define the continuous regulators r_HK from D(H^{r+1},O_F), r_log from D(H^{r+1},Z_p), and r_dR from D(H^{r+1},O_K) by integrating the corresponding first Chern classes of §7 and their cup products. Diagrams (6.29)–(6.31) factor them through the continuous Steinberg duals. In the Hyodo–Kato diagram the resulting map Sp^cont_r(O_F)^* → H^0_ét(Y,WΩ^r) is continuous and injective and its rational composite is the canonical inclusion into Sp_r(F)^*. The target is compact over O_F because k is finite; bounded vectors, Corollary 5.3 and the nonzero mod-p symbol give the integral isomorphism, whose reduction is over k, not k̄. The logarithmic diagram compares H^0_ét(Y,WΩ^r_log) with the φ=p^r part of H^r_ét(Y,WΩ^•). The de Rham diagram uses H^r_dR(X)⊗_{O_K}K → H^r_dR(X_K); the generic fibre is essential. Lemma 6.32 separately identifies the logarithmic groups on Y and Ȳ. These three diagrams must be separate proof leaves in a completed extraction.
items.note: The mod p irreducibility of Sp_r(F_p) (Grosse-Klönne) is the pivot: it turns a non-zero map into an isomorphism, which is how an integral statement is extracted from a rational one.

items.name: Lemma 6.32 and Remark 6.33: base change k → k̄ for logarithmic forms, and the integral Hyodo–Kato isomorphism
items.statement: For n ≥ 1 the canonical maps H^0_ét(Y,W_nΩ^r_log) → H^0_ét(Ȳ,W_nΩ^r_log) and H^0_ét(Y,WΩ^r_log) → H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^r_log) are topological isomorphisms: by dévissage one reduces to n = 1, where H^0_ét(Ȳ,Ω^r_log) ≅ H^0_ét(Ȳ,Ω^r)^{C=1}, étale base change gives H^0_ét(Ȳ,Ω^r) ≅ H^0_ét(Y,Ω^r) ⊗̂_k k̄, and C = 1 on logarithmic forms. Moreover, defining ι_HK by requiring the regulator diagram with r_HK and r_dR to commute, one obtains a continuous map which is compatible with the bounded and the overconvergent Hyodo–Kato maps, and since Sp^cont_r(O_F)^* ⊗_{O_F} O_K ≅ Sp^cont_r(O_K)^*, an integral Hyodo–Kato topological isomorphism ι_HK : H^r_ét(Y,WΩ^•) ⊗_{O_F} O_K ≅ H^r_dR(X).
items.note: The introduction calls this integral Hyodo–Kato isomorphism "a bit surprising"; it is what makes γ′_HK surjective in Corollary 6.42, and hence what makes the étale computation work at all.

items.name: Lemma 6.34: Frobenius eigenspaces of absolute crystalline cohomology through Hyodo–Kato cohomology
items.statement: Let X be a semistable Stein formal scheme over O_K and r ≥ 0. There are compatible natural strict quasi-isomorphisms ι_cr : [RΓ_cr(X_{O_C})_{Q_p}]^{φ=p^r} ≅ [(RΓ_cr(X_0/O^0_F) ⊗̂_{O_F} Â_st)_{Q_p}]^{N=0,φ=p^r} in the geometric case, and [RΓ_cr(X)_{Q_p}]^{φ=p^r} ≅ [RΓ_cr(X_0/O^0_F)_{Q_p}]^{N=0,φ=p^r} in the arithmetic case. The proof uses the strict quasi-isomorphism [RΓ_cr(X_n/r^PD_{ϖ,n}) ⊗̂_{r^PD_{ϖ,n}} Â_{st,n}]^{N=0} ≅ RΓ_cr(X_n) of §3.3.3 and then, adapting the proof of Theorem 4.1 and the p^N-inverse argument of Proposition 6.1, the map h_cr, whose error terms have cohomology killed by p^N with N depending only on r and dim X_0.
items.note: This is the integral analogue of Theorem 4.1: it is what replaces the pro-étale Bloch–Kato route in the étale computation.

items.name: The Bloch–Kato presentation of the integral syntomic cohomology and the map γ_HK
items.statement: From the filtered comparison ι^2_BK : (RΓ_dR(X) ⊗̂_{O_K} A_cr,K)_{Q_p}/F^r ≅ RΓ_cr(X_{O_C})_{Q_p}/F^r and from ι_cr one sets γ_HK := (ι^2_BK)^{-1} ι_cr^{-1} and obtains a natural strict quasi-isomorphism RΓ_syn(X_{O_C},Z_p(r))_{Q_p} ≅ [[(RΓ_cr(X_0/O^0_F) ⊗̂_{O_F} Â_st)_{Q_p}]^{N=0,φ=p^r} —γ_HK→ (RΓ_dR(X) ⊗̂_{O_K} A_cr,K)_{Q_p}/F^r], compatible with its pro-étale analogue: there is a natural continuous map of distinguished triangles from this to RΓ_syn(X_{O_C},Q_p(r)) → [RΓ_cr(X_0/O^0_F,F) ⊗̂^R_F B̂^+_st]^{N=0,φ=p^r} —γ_HK→ (RΓ_dR(X_K) ⊗̂^R_K B^+_dR)/F^r.
items.note: In general γ_HK is hard to identify; for the Drinfeld half-space both its source and its target simplify by the acyclicity of the differentials, which is the whole point of §6.

items.name: Lemma 6.37: the Hyodo–Kato part of the syntomic cohomology of the half-space
items.statement: For the standard model X and Y=X_0, the cohomology of [(RΓ_cr(Y/O_F^0)⊗̂_{O_F}Â_st)_{Q_p}]^{N=0,φ=p^r} is classical. Its degree-r term is H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^r_log)⊗Q_p and its degree-(r−1) term is (H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^{r−1}_log)⊗̂_{Z_p}A_cr^{φ=p})⊗Q_p. Proposition 6.23 and the Mittag–Leffler argument give RΓ_cr(Y/O_F^0)⊗̂_{O_F}Â_st ≃ ⊕_i(H^0_ét(Y,WΩ^i)⊗̂_{O_F}Â_st)[−i] ≃ ⊕_i(H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^i)⊗̂_{W(k̄)}Â_st)[−i]. Taking derived N=0 and then φ=p^r gives the logarithmic description. For A=H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^i_log), A is a countable product of finite free Z_p-modules after replacing the inverse system by its eventual images; Frobenius on the degree-i contribution acts by p^i. Hence (A⊗̂_{Z_p}A_cr)^{φ=p^j}=A⊗̂_{Z_p}A_cr^{φ=p^{j−i}} for j≥i. The p^i-surjectivity in (6.41) removes the higher derived obstruction after inverting p. Keep the shift [−i] and the change from O_F to W(k̄) explicit.
items.note: This is (1.13) of the introduction. The pointwise description of H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^i_log) as a countable product of finite free Z_p-modules is what makes the eigenspace computation possible.

items.name: Corollary 6.42: the syntomic cohomology of the half-space in degree r, and the surjectivity of γ′_HK
items.statement: For r ≥ 0 the r-th cohomology of RΓ_syn(X_{O_C},Z_p(r))_{Q_p} is classical and there is a natural topological isomorphism H^r(RΓ_syn(X_{O_C},Z_p(r))_{Q_p}) ≅ H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^r_log) ⊗ Q_p. Proposition 6.23 identifies the de Rham term with ⊕_{r−1 ≥ i ≥ 0}(H^0(X,Ω^i) ⊗̂_{O_K}(A_cr,K/F^{r−i}))[−i], so γ_HK becomes γ′_HK : (H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^{r−1}_log) ⊗̂_{Z_p} A_cr^{φ=p}) ⊗ Q_p → (H^0(X,Ω^{r−1}) ⊗̂_{O_K} O_C) ⊗ Q_p and one gets the long exact sequence ending in H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^r_log) ⊗ Q_p → 0. Its strict surjectivity is proved by factoring it through ι_HK ⊗ ι and θ and reducing to the map γ_C : (H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^{r−1}_log) ⊗̂_{Z_p} O_C) ⊗ Q_p → (H^0(X,Ω^{r−1}) ⊗̂_{O_K} O_C) ⊗ Q_p, which is an isomorphism because H^{r−1}_dR(X) → H^{r−1}_dR(X_K) is injective (Proposition 6.27) and the integral Hyodo–Kato map is a topological isomorphism (Remark 6.33); strictness follows because θ : A_cr^{φ=p} → O_C has a continuous Z_p-linear section.
items.note: This is the surjectivity the introduction calls "a bit surprising"; it is the step where the integral Hyodo–Kato isomorphism is indispensable.

items.name: Corollary 6.44: the p-adic étale cohomology of the half-space is logarithmic de Rham–Witt cohomology
items.statement: For r ≥ 0 the cohomology H̃^r_ét(X_C,Q_p(r)) is classical and there is a natural topological isomorphism H^r_ét(X_C,Q_p(r)) ≅ H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^r_log)_{Q_p}, compatible with the étale and the logarithmic de Rham–Witt Chern classes. It follows from Proposition 6.1 and Corollary 6.42, the compatibility from that of the étale, syntomic, crystalline, c^{st}_1, crystalline Hyodo–Kato and logarithmic de Rham–Witt Chern classes of §7.
items.note: The bridge between the syntomic computation and the étale answer.

items.name: Theorem 6.45: the main theorem of §6 — étale cohomology, its integral avatars, the regulators and the G-bounded description
items.statement: Let r ≥ 0. (1) There is a natural topological isomorphism of G × G_K-modules H^r_ét(X_C,Q_p(r)) ≅ Sp^cont_r(Q_p)^* ≅ Sp_r(Z_p)^* ⊗ Q_p. (2) There are natural topological isomorphisms of G-modules H^r_dR(X)_K ≅ Sp^cont_r(K)^*, H^r_cr(Y/O^0_F)_{Q_p} ≅ Sp^cont_r(F)^*, and H^i_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^r_{Ȳ,log})_{Q_p} ≅ Sp^cont_r(Q_p)^* for i = 0 and 0 for i > 0. (3) The regulators r_dR : M(H^{r+1},K) → H^r_dR(X)_K, r_HK : M(H^{r+1},F) → H^r_cr(Y/O^0_F)_{Q_p} and r_log : M(H^{r+1},Q_p) → H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^r_log)_{Q_p} are strict surjective maps of weak duals of Banach spaces, equivariant and compatible with the isomorphisms of (1) and (2), and their kernels are exactly the degenerate measures. (4) The natural map H^r_ét(X_C,Q_p(r)) → H^r_proét(X_C,Q_p(r)) is injective and identifies étale cohomology with the G-bounded vectors of pro-étale cohomology. Part (4) uses that (Sp_r(Q_p)^*)^{G-bd} ≅ Sp^cont_r(Q_p)^* and that (dΩ^{r−1}(X_C))^{G-bd} = 0, which reduces to the injectivity of (Ω^r(X_K)^{d=0})^{G-bd} → H^r_dR(X_K) and then to Ω^r(X) ⊗̂_{O_K} K ≅ Ω^r(X_K)^{G-bd}, valid because X is covered by G-translates of an open U with U_K affinoid.
items.note: This is Theorem 1.3(1) and (3). Remark 6.46 announces the étale regulator r_ét in the sequel [18]. As printed, the three regulators of part (3) and the one of Remark 6.46 are written on measures on H^{d+1} rather than H^{r+1}; recorded in sourceIssues. Independent review: Source issue E33 corrects the proof’s degree: dΩ^{r−1} consists of exact r-forms. Use bounded closed r-forms and Proposition 6.27 in degree r.

items.name: Appendix A: a second proof of Corollary 6.25 avoiding the ordinarity of the truncations
items.statement: Let X/k^0 be a fine log scheme of Cartier type, Z^j_∞ := ∩_n Z^j_n and B^j_∞ := ∪_n B^j_n as subsheaves of Ω^j, so that Z^j_∞ is the sheaf of forms ω with dC^nω = 0 for all n, carries the Cartier operator C, and satisfies B^j_∞ = ∪_n (Z^j_∞)^{C^n=0} and Ω^j_log = (Z^j_∞)^{C=1}. Lemma A.1: if X/k^0 is semistable and k is algebraically closed then B^j_∞ ⊕ (Ω^j_log ⊗_{F_p} k) → Z^j_∞ is an isomorphism of étale sheaves; the proof restricts to a dense smooth open, where Raynaud's theorem makes Z^i_∞(U) a union of finite dimensional C-stable k-vector spaces, and applies the semilinear algebra decomposition E = E_nilp ⊕ E_inv with E^{C=1} ⊗_{F_p} k ≅ E_inv, which is where the algebraic closure of k is crucial. Lemma A.2: H^0_ét(Ȳ,B^j_∞) = 0, proved by mapping to the product over the irreducible components — injectively, since H^0_ét(Ȳ,Ω^j) injects into that product — and using that on the quasi-compact central component H^0_ét(T,B^j_∞) = colim_n H^0_ét(T,B^j_n) = 0. Together these give Corollary 6.25(1) in degree 0; in higher degrees one uses the exact sequence 0 → Ω^j_log → Ω^j/B^j_1 —1−C^{-1}→ Ω^j/B^j_2 → 0 and the surjectivity of 1 − C^{-1} on H^0_ét(Ȳ,Ω^j), which follows from the Artin–Schreier sequence for k̄ and the Mittag-Leffler property of the system H^0_ét(Ȳ_s^∘,Ω^j_log); part (2) then follows by induction on n from the two Verschiebung sequences.
items.locator: Appendix A, pp. 63–65 (Remark 6.26, p. 51, announces it)
items.note: The appendix replaces the ordinarity of the Y_s by the Illusie–Raynaud structure theory of Z^j_∞; it is the part of the paper that the published version keeps as an appendix and that the Springer landing page lists as "Alternative proof of Corollary 6.25".

items.name: The p^N-inverse of the linearised crystalline Frobenius, and Lemma 7.3
items.statement: Let Y be a quasi-compact semistable formal scheme over O_K and d = dim Y_0. The linearised Frobenius maps r^PD_{ϖ,n,φ} ⊗^L_{r^PD_{ϖ,n}} RΓ_cr(Y_1/r^PD_{ϖ,n}) → RΓ_cr(Y_1/r^PD_{ϖ,n}) and O_{F,n,φ} ⊗^L_{O_{F,n}} RΓ_cr(Y_0/O^0_{F,n}) → RΓ_cr(Y_0/O^0_{F,n}) admit a p^N-inverse ψ, with φψ = ψφ = p^N for N = N(d) (Hyodo–Kato 2.24). Lemma 7.3: the projection p_0 : RΓ_cr(Y/r^PD_{ϖ,n}) → RΓ_cr(Y_0/O^0_{F,n}) admits a map ι_{ϖ,n} in the other direction which is functorial in the formal scheme and in n, Frobenius-equivariant and a p^{N_ι}-section, and whose r^PD_{ϖ,n}-linearisation RΓ_cr(Y_0/O^0_{F,n}) ⊗^L_{O_{F,n}} r^PD_{ϖ,n} → RΓ_cr(Y/r^PD_{ϖ,n}) is a p^N-quasi-isomorphism with N = N(d,e). It is obtained from the case K = F (Hyodo–Kato, Prop. 4.13, with its section ι_{p,n} of p_0 over r^PD_{p,n}) by setting ι_{ϖ,n} := g^*ι_{p,n}ψ^e, where g : Spec r^PD_{ϖ,n} → Spec r^PD_{p,n} is T ↦ T^{p^e}, a ↦ φ^e(a); the mechanism is that Frobenius is close to an isomorphism on the special fibre and close to zero on the divided-power ideal.
items.locator: proof of Proposition 7.1 and Lemma 7.3, §7.1, pp. 59–60
items.note: Write a(d) for the unramified exponent and b(d) for the Frobenius-inverse exponent. The ramified construction gives M(d,e)=a(d)+e b(d); take the final N_ι=M(d,e). This satisfies the lemma’s stated dependence on (d,e). E20 is rejected. The wrong base r^PD_{ϖ,n} in the unramified section remains E19.

items.name: The twisted Hyodo–Kato map ι̃_HK and its independence of choices modulo p^N
items.statement: With ρ : RΓ_dR(Y) ≅ RΓ_cr(Y/O^×_K) the canonical comparison and p_ϖ the base change T ↦ ϖ, set ι̃_HK := ρ^{-1} p_ϖ ι_ϖ, where ι_ϖ := holim_n ι_{ϖ,n}. Then ι̃_HK : RΓ_cr(Y_0/O^0_F) ⊗_{O_F} O_K → RΓ_dR(Y) is a p^N-quasi-isomorphism with N = N(d,e), and modulo p^N it is independent of the choices made. For quasi-compact Y the Hyodo–Kato map is defined as ι_HK := p^{−N_ι} ι̃_HK, giving the Hyodo–Kato topological isomorphism (H^i_cr(Y_0/O^0_F) ⊗_{O_F} O_K) ⊗ K ≅ H^i_dR(Y) ⊗ K.
items.note: This is the classical Hyodo–Kato isomorphism of Hyodo–Kato, made functorial and quantitative; the "bounded" version — with the de Rham cohomology of the formal model rather than of the generic fibre — is what §6 needs.

items.name: Proposition 7.1 and (7.5): the two Hyodo–Kato isomorphisms in the Stein case
items.statement: Let X be a semistable Stein weak formal scheme over O_K with associated formal scheme X̂. For every r ≥ 0 there are compatible Hyodo–Kato topological isomorphisms ι_HK : H^r_cr(X_0/O^0_F,F) ⊗_F K ≅ H^r_dR(X̂_K) and ι_HK : (H^r_cr(X_0/O^0_F) ⊗_{O_F} O_K) ⊗ K ≅ H^r_dR(X̂) ⊗ K, defined as the inverse limits over a Stein covering {U_s} of the quasi-compact maps for the pieces X̂|_{U_s} (the second after dividing by p^{N_ι}). The limits are legitimate because of the topological isomorphisms H^i_cr(X_0/O^0_F,F) ≅ lim←_s H^i_cr(U_s/O^0_F,F), H^i_cr(X_0/O^0_F) ≅ lim←_s H^i_cr(U_s/O^0_F), H^i_dR(X̂_K) ≅ lim←_s H^i_dR(]U_s[_{X̂_K}) and H^i_dR(X̂) ⊗ Q_p ≅ (lim←_s H^i_dR(X̂|_{U_s})) ⊗ Q_p, the first two from the Mittag-Leffler property of the systems over the Y_s and the last from the p^N-isomorphism property of ι̃_HK together with that Mittag-Leffler property.
items.note: The second isomorphism — bounded Hyodo–Kato against bounded de Rham cohomology — is the one used in Proposition 6.27 and Remark 6.33.

items.name: Corollary 7.6: compatibility with Grosse-Klönne's overconvergent Hyodo–Kato isomorphism
items.statement: For X a semistable Stein weak formal scheme over O_K and all i, the diagram with rows H^i_rig(X_0/O^0_F) → H^i_dR(X_K) (Grosse-Klönne), H^i_cr(X_0/O^0_F,F) → H^i_dR(X̂_K) and H^i_cr(X_0/O^0_F)_{Q_p} → H^i_dR(X̂)_{Q_p} (Proposition 7.1), all horizontal maps Hyodo–Kato isomorphisms after the appropriate linearisation and all vertical maps the canonical comparisons, commutes. The proof works locally, with X quasi-compact, on a diagram whose dotted arrows are p^{−N_ι}ι_ϖ, and reduces to the commutativity of that dotted part, which follows because all maps are Frobenius-compatible, H^i_rig(X_0/O^0_F) is finite dimensional, and Frobenius on T is highly nilpotent.
items.note: This is what allows the paper to use the overconvergent Hyodo–Kato isomorphism for the pro-étale computation and the bounded one for the étale computation, and to compare the two answers (which is needed for Theorem 1.3(3)).

items.name: The log structure of a semistable formal scheme is canonical, so M^gp(U) = O(U_K)^*
items.statement: For X a semistable formal scheme over O_K with sheaf of monoids M and group completion M^gp, the log structure is canonical in Berkovich's sense: for every open U, M(U) = {x ∈ O_X(U) : x_K ∈ O^*_{X_K}(U_K)}, the functions on the model that are invertible on the generic fibre; this holds also with self-intersections. Consequently M^gp(U) = O(U_K)^*.
items.note: This identification is what makes every Chern class map below a map out of the units of the generic fibre, which is what lets the symbols of the K-rational hyperplanes be used.

items.name: The crystalline, Hyodo–Kato, logarithmic de Rham–Witt and de Rham first Chern classes
items.statement: On X_ét there are the crystalline first Chern class maps of complexes of sheaves c^{st}_1 : M^gp → M^gp_n → Rε_* J^{[1]}_{X_n/r^PD_{ϖ,n}}[1] and c^{HK}_1 : M^gp → M^gp_0 → Rε_* J^{[1]}_{X_0/O^0_{F,n}}[1] (Tsuji 2.2.3), where ε is the projection from the crystalline-étale site to the étale site; they are compatible, the second being the T ↦ 0 reduction of the first. Taking global sections and holim gives functorial maps c^{st}_1, c^{HK}_1 : H^0(X_K,O^*_{X_K}) → RΓ_cr(X/r^PD_ϖ,J^{[1]})[1] resp. RΓ_cr(X_0/O^0_F,J^{[1]})[1]. The Hyodo–Kato classes can also be defined with de Rham–Witt complexes, giving compatible c^{log}_1 : H^0(X_K,O^*) → RΓ_ét(X_0,WΩ^•_{X_0,log})[1] and c^{HK}_1 : H^0(X_K,O^*) → RΓ_ét(X_0,WΩ^•_{X_0})[1] (de Shalit 2.1), compatible with the crystalline ones by Gros's construction with O^* replaced by M^gp. There is also the de Rham class c^{dR}_1 : M^gp → M^gp_n —dlog→ Ω^•_{X_n/O^×_{K,n}}[1], giving c^{dR}_1 : H^0(X_K,O^*) → RΓ_dR(X)[1], compatible via RΓ_dR(X) → RΓ_dR(X_K) with the rigid analytic class defined by dlog; and for a semistable weak formal scheme the overconvergent classes c^{HK}_1 : H^0(X_K,O^*) → RΓ_rig(X_0/O^0_F)[1] and c^{dR}_1 : H^0(X_K,O^*) → RΓ_dR(X_K)[1], compatible with the previous ones. So a symbol is the first Chern class of an invertible function on the generic fibre, living in degree 1, and cup products of r symbols give classes in degree r.
items.note: These symbol maps are what the regulators of §5.4 and §6.3 integrate, and what makes every comparison in the paper compatible with the standard symbols of the K-rational hyperplanes. The atlas plans p-adic regulators at PadicHodgeRegulators D.2/D.5 in the smooth good-reduction setting, but not Chern classes of units on a semistable formal scheme in the logarithmic crystalline, de Rham–Witt and overconvergent theories.

items.name: Lemma 7.8: the Hyodo–Kato isomorphisms are compatible with the first Chern classes
items.statement: Let X be a semistable Stein weak formal scheme over O_K. The three Hyodo–Kato maps ι_HK : H^1_cr(X_0/O^0_F) ⊗ Q_p → H^1_dR(X̂) ⊗ Q_p, ι_HK : H^1_cr(X_0/O^0_F,F) → H^1_dR(X̂_K) and ι_HK : H^1_rig(X_0/O^0_F) → H^1_dR(X_K) (the first two of Proposition 7.1, the third Grosse-Klönne's) satisfy ι_HK ∘ c^{HK}_1 = c^{dR}_1 on the units of the corresponding generic fibre. The proof writes ι_HK = ρ^{-1}p_ϖι′_ϖ with ι′_ϖ := p^{−N_ι}ι_ϖ, notes that ζ := ι′_ϖ(c^{HK}_1(x)) − c^{st}_1(x) lies in ker p_0, and shows ζ = 0: the linearisation β : (H^1_cr(X_0/O^0_F) ⊗ Q_p) ⊗̂_F r^PD_{ϖ,Q_p} → H^1_cr(X/r^PD_ϖ) ⊗ Q_p is an isomorphism, so ζ = β(ζ′) with ζ′ in the ideal part; since ι′_ϖ is Frobenius-compatible and φ(c^{HK}_1(x)) = p c^{HK}_1(x), φ(c^{st}_1(x)) = p c^{st}_1(x), one gets φ^n(ζ′) = p^n ζ′, and as φ^n maps the n-th ideal I_0 into I_n one finds ζ′ ∈ ∩_n (⋯) ⊗̂_F I_{n,Q_p} = 0. The third map follows from the first two through Corollary 7.6.
items.note: This is the compatibility used in the proof of Lemma 5.11 and in §4.3.2, and the reason the Hyodo–Kato cohomology of the half-space can be pinned down by symbols. It is the analogue of Nekovář–Nizioł, Lemma 5.1.

items.name: Existing strict linear-map carrier
items.statement: For a map between topological spaces, Topology.IsStrictMap f means IsQuotientMap of its range factorization. For linear maps between the stated topological modules, Mathlib identifies this with an open quotient onto the range and with a homeomorphism M/ker(f) ≃ range(f). This does not construct the paper’s exact category.
items.note: Supplier statement read at Mathlib 082e2d3 / Tau Ceti f790474; no new formalization claimed.

items.name: Existing Tate-ring open mapping and strictness implications
items.statement: Let A be a commutative topological Tate ring. Let M,N be complete uniform additive groups with countably generated uniformities, A-modules, M nonarchimedean with continuous scalar action, and N T0 with continuous constant scalar multiplication. A linear map f:M→N continuous at zero is open and a quotient map if surjective; if its range is closed it is strict. These are the exact Tau Ceti implications; the LF theorem and the paper’s exact-category construction are separate.
items.note: Supplier statement read at Mathlib 082e2d3 / Tau Ceti f790474; no new formalization claimed.

routes.title: Cohomology comparisons, Part II: syntomic comparison for semistable Stein spaces
routes.reason: The nonproper Stein comparison extends the direction of CohomologyComparisons beyond CP.4’s proper semistable theorem. This is a provisional Part II, not a separate foundational direction. The candidate identifier is retained for cross-paper references, but the route is rejected pending splitting off dagger geometry already owned by AdicSpacesPartII F1, ordinary rigid cohomology at RD.3–5, new log-rigid/HK contracts in the CrystallineCohomology direction, and the generic functional-analysis supplier. The currently grouped items are not all construction tasks for this owner.
routes.brief: Final theorems, as the paper states them. (1) The comparison theorem (Theorem 1.8 = Theorem 4.12): for X a semistable Stein weak formal scheme over O_K and r ≥ 0, a G_K-equivariant map of strictly exact sequences of Fréchet spaces from 0 → Ω^{r−1}(X_C)/ker d → H^r_proét(X_C,Q_p(r)) → (H^r_HK(X_0) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{N=0,φ=p^r} → 0 to 0 → Ω^{r−1}(X_C)/ker d → Ω^r(X_C)^{d=0} → H^r_dR(X_C) → 0, with β̃ and ι_HK ⊗ θ strict with closed images and ker β̃ ≅ (H^r_HK(X_0) ⊗̂_F B^+_st)^{N=0,φ=p^{r−1}}; equivalently (Remark 4.13) H^r_proét is the pullback of the Hyodo–Kato term and Ω^r(X_C)^{d=0} over H^r_dR(X_C) — a one-way comparison, to be contrasted with the proper case (4.14), which is CP.4's theorem. (2) The overconvergent package it needs: dagger algebras and dagger spaces, weak formal schemes and weak completions, partially proper and Stein dagger spaces and the equivalence of partially proper dagger and rigid spaces, semistable weak formal schemes, Stein with semistable reduction with its exhaustion {U_s},{Y_s} by ideally log-smooth proper pieces, and idealized log-schemes. (3) Overconvergent log-rigid and Hyodo–Kato cohomology after Grosse-Klönne: RΓ_rig(Y/O^0_F) and RΓ_rig(Y/O^×_K) built from embedding systems, exactifications and tubes as a hocolim over hypercovers; Frobenius, the monodromy N = Res(∇(dlog 0)) and Nφ = pφN; finiteness, the canonical Hausdorff topology and mixedness (Proposition 3.2) through the weight spectral sequence; strictness of the de Rham differentials on a smooth Stein or affinoid dagger space (Lemma 3.4); the compactified deformation spaces (P^{J′}_M,V^{J′}_M) and the two specialisations T ↦ 0, T ↦ ϖ (Propositions 3.9 and 3.12); and the Hyodo–Kato isomorphism ι_HK : RΓ_HK(X_0) ⊗_F K ≅ RΓ_dR(X_K) as a zigzag, with its dependence on ϖ. (4) Overconvergent syntomic cohomology: the period rings r^+_ϖ, r^PD_ϖ, Â_st, B̂^+_st with Â_st,n ≅ RΓ_cr(O^×_{C,n}/r^PD_{ϖ,n}) and B^+_st ≅ B̂^{+,N-nilp}_st, A_cr,K and the map ι : B̂^+_st → B^+_dR; the derived eigenspace [·]^{N=0,φ=p^r} as a homotopy limit; RΓ_syn(X_C,Q_p(r)) = [HK(X_C,r) → DR(X_C,r)]; the computations of both terms (Example 3.16, Lemmas 3.20, 3.26, 3.28, Example 3.30) with the two fundamental exact sequences and the trivialisation exp(Nu); and the fundamental diagram (Proposition 3.36) with Lemma 3.39 and the slope bound. (5) Crystalline syntomic cohomology: the Fontaine–Messing complexes and period maps (Propositions 3.45, 6.1 and Corollary 3.46, with the p^N-inverse and the p^{−r} twist that makes them compatible with Chern classes), the Bloch–Kato variant and the Künneth comparison ι_BK (Proposition 3.48), and the comparison ι_rig of the two syntomic theories for Stein spaces (Theorem 4.1) with convergent cohomology, the change-of-topology map and the map h_cr. (6) The examples: rigid affine space (Proposition 4.17), the torus, and Stein curves — with the semistable models of Fresnel–van der Put and the blow-up construction they need. (7) The symbols of §7: the canonical log structure with M^gp(U) = O(U_K)^*, the crystalline, Hyodo–Kato, logarithmic de Rham–Witt, de Rham and overconvergent first Chern classes, the bounded Hyodo–Kato isomorphisms (Proposition 7.1) with their compatibility with Grosse-Klönne's (Corollary 7.6), and the compatibility of ι_HK with the Chern classes (Lemma 7.8). Import the period rings and their normalisation from CohomologyComparisons CP.0 and PadicHodgeTheory R06.1, the proper Hyodo–Kato complex with φ and N from CrystallineCohomology CR.6, log structures from CR.5, the syntomic mapping fibre and the p-adic regulator formalism from PadicHodgeRegulators D.2, the pro-étale site from AdicEtaleGeometry A1, formal models and nearby cycles from ClassicalAdicEtaleCohomology H1, Banach–Colmez spaces and their Dimension formalism from VectorBundlesAndIsocrystals VB3, and the convergent-cohomology package from the Part II that PAPER-KISIN-MADAPUSIPERA-SHIN-22 proposes under CrystallineCohomology. Do not plan the functional analysis here: it is the Part II below. Do not plan the Drinfeld half-space computation here: it is the next route. Independent review boundary: the dagger/ordinary-rigid/log-HK/functional-analysis portions above are imports or separately owned continuation contracts, not duplicate constructions in this Part II. Separate these item bundles and their APIs before design; this provisional routing is rejected.

independentReview.reason: Reject the remaining bundled scope after the Part II correction. AdicSpacesPartII F1 already owns dagger algebras, spaces and overconvergent de Rham complexes; RD.3–5 owns ordinary rigid frames/cohomology. CR.5–6, CP.0/4 and the proposed convergent Part II are separate suppliers. Put the genuinely nonproper syntomic comparison in a CohomologyComparisons continuation and the new log-rigid/HK scope in a CrystallineCohomology continuation, coordinating the Colmez–Nizioł 2017 route. The 44-item bundle has no complete definition APIs, tests or supplier closure.

routes.title: Drinfeld symmetric spaces, generalized Steinberg representations and their p-adic cohomology
routes.reason: The Drinfeld cohomology computation is a candidate application route shared with CDN21. ET.6a already constructs Drinfeld towers for arbitrary n, so its geometric foundations must be imported and compared with this paper’s particular standard model. Generic smooth representations and induction belong to SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups; buildings belong to RG2.2; locally analytic representation theory joins the Ding proposal. The special logarithmic-form, regulator and p-adic cohomology computations still need precise ownership after those shared imports. The current brief is rejected for bundling the generic foundations with the application and lacking proof/API closure.
routes.brief: Final theorems, as the paper states them. (1) Theorem 1.3: for every r ≥ 0, H^r_ét(H^d_C,Q_p(r)) ≅ Sp^cont_r(Q_p)^* as G × G_K-modules (weak duals of Banach spaces); a strictly exact sequence of G × G_K-Fréchet spaces 0 → Ω^{r−1}(H^d_C)/ker d → H^r_proét(H^d_C,Q_p(r)) → Sp_r(Q_p)^* → 0 (Theorem 5.13); and the identification of étale cohomology with the G-bounded vectors of pro-étale cohomology (Theorem 6.45(4)). (2) The representation theory: the profinite flag spaces X_J = G/P_J, the generalized Steinberg representations Sp_J(A) = LC(X_J,A)/Σ_i LC(X_{J∪{i}},A) with Sp_r := Sp_{{1,…,d−r}}, their continuous and locally analytic variants, the LF/nuclear-Fréchet topologies on them and on their duals, the theorem of Casselman and Grosse-Klönne that the Sp_J are the irreducible constituents of LC(G/B,A) in characteristics 0 and p (and its failure for ℓ ≠ p), the uniqueness of the G-stable lattice (Corollary 5.3), the universal unitary completion and the G-bounded vectors (Corollary 5.4), and the mod p irreducibility of Sp_r(F_p). (3) The geometry: the standard G-equivariant semistable weak formal model of H^d_K, the bijection between the vertices of the Bruhat–Tits building of PGL_{d+1}(K) and the irreducible components of its special fibre, the truncations Y_s, Y_s^∘, the central component T as an iterated blow-up of P^d_k with its divisors, and the Stein exhaustion U_n of the half-space. (4) The Schneider–Stuhler package: the simplicial profinite sets Y^{(r)}_•, T^{(r)}_• (the Tits building) and N T^{(r)}_•, the computation H̃^{r−1}(|T^{(r)}_•|,Z) ≅ Sp_r(Z) with the vanishing outside degrees 0 and r−1, the support spectral sequence and the homotopy axiom, and Theorem 5.8 for ℓ-adic étale, pro-étale and de Rham cohomology, with Corollary 5.9 for the G-bounded part of the de Rham cohomology. (5) Symbols and regulators: the cocycle space LC_c(H^{r+1},Z) ≅ Sp_r(Z), distributions and measures on H^{r+1}, degenerate distributions, the hyperplane symbols and the regulators r_dR, r_ét, r_proét, r_HK, r_log with the strict exactness of Iovita–Spiess (Theorem 5.10) and its Hyodo–Kato generalisation (Lemma 5.11 and (5.12)), the triviality of N and the action of Frobenius by q^r. (6) The étale computation: the acyclicity of the sheaves of differentials on T, on the model and on the truncations (Grosse-Klönne) with the acyclicity criterion for coefficient systems on the truncated building; ordinary log schemes with the criteria of Bloch–Kato, Illusie–Raynaud and Lorenzon, the ordinarity of projective bundles and blow-ups, the criterion from acyclicity (Lemma 6.13) and the pro-ordinarity of the special fibre (Corollary 6.18); the de Rham–Witt vanishing and Verschiebung sequences (Lemma 6.20); Proposition 6.23 and Corollary 6.25 identifying H^0_ét(Ȳ,WΩ^r_log) ⊗̂ W(k̄) with the de Rham–Witt cohomology; the injectivity statements of Proposition 6.27; Theorem 6.28 and the three integral regulator diagrams; the integral Hyodo–Kato isomorphism (Remark 6.33); the syntomic computation (Lemmas 6.34, 6.37 and Corollary 6.42) and the main theorems (Corollary 6.44 and Theorem 6.45). (7) The appendix: the sheaves Z^j_∞, B^j_∞, the splitting Z^j_∞ ≅ B^j_∞ ⊕ (Ω^j_log ⊗_{F_p} k̄) over an algebraically closed field and the Artin–Schreier argument, giving a second proof of Corollary 6.25 that avoids the ordinarity of the truncations. Import the comparison theorem and the whole syntomic machine from the first route above, the towers and period morphisms from ET.6a, the parabolic and Bruhat–Tits structure theory from ReductiveGroupsPartII RG2.2, the de Rham–Witt complex with F, V and dlog from CrystallineCohomology CR.4, and the locally analytic Steinberg representation with the Orlik–Strauch and Orlik–Schraen theorems from the roadmap proposed by PAPER-DING-25. Do not plan the integral (F_p-coefficient) statement: the paper only announces it, and it is proved in the sequel, PAPER-COLMEZ-DOSPINESCU-NIZIOL-21.

independentReview.reason: Reject the brief as written. ET.6a constructs Drinfeld towers for arbitrary n, so the claim that the atlas stops at dimension one is false. Import base geometry and compare the standard semistable model explicitly. Generic smooth induction/Steinberg constructions extend SmoothRepresentationsOfLocalGroups, and buildings come from RG2.2. Retain a possible Drinfeld cohomology application route only after these boundaries and the CDN21 shared identifier are settled. Split the bundled §§5–6 and Appendix statements and correct Y versus Ȳ before design.

routes.title: Locally analytic distributions, Part II: quasi-abelian p-adic functional analysis and derived categories of convex spaces
routes.reason: LocallyAnalyticDistributions builds Banach spaces of locally analytic functions, the locally convex inductive-limit topology on C^la(X,K), continuous duals and projective systems of Banach duals (L0), and the Amice transform with its Fréchet comparison (L1). That is the same direction — p-adic functional analysis — but it stops short of everything §2 of this paper needs: the quasi-abelian category C_K of locally convex K-vector spaces with its exact structure, strictness, the t-structure of Schneiders with its left and right hearts, the notion of classical cohomology, the completed tensor product with its exactness and its derived version, acyclic inductive systems, and the integral category of pro-discrete O_K-modules with the rationalisation functor and its derived functors. These are new layers in the parent's direction rather than a new roadmap, and they are what every topological statement in this paper and in its companions is proved in. Mathlib already has the notion of a strict map (Topology.IsStrictMap) and Tau Ceti the open mapping theorem and the closed-range criterion over a Tate ring (TauCeti.Huber.IsTateRing.isOpenMap, isStrictMap_of_isClosed_range), so the layer starts from those.
routes.brief: Final theorems, as the paper states them (§2, pp. 7–13). (1) The category C_K of locally convex K-vector spaces (not assumed separated) with continuous linear maps: kernels, cokernels, images and coimages computed with the induced topologies, quasi-abelianness, and the two elementary observations on separatedness and finite-dimensional targets. (2) Strictness: a morphism is strict iff it is relatively open iff coim → im is an isomorphism; the exact structure whose admissible monomorphisms are embeddings and admissible epimorphisms open surjections; strict complexes, strictly exact sequences, strictly acyclic complexes and strict quasi-isomorphisms. Build these on Mathlib's Topology.IsStrictMap and on Tau Ceti's Tate-ring open mapping theorem and closed-range criterion, and add the LF version: a continuous surjection between countable inductive limits of Fréchet spaces is open. (3) Lemma 2.1: a complex of Banach or of Fréchet spaces with trivial algebraic cohomology is strictly acyclic, and an algebraic quasi-isomorphism between such complexes is a strict quasi-isomorphism. (4) The homological algebra: truncations, the cohomology objects H̃^n = (coim d^{n−1} → ker d^n), the derived ∞-category D(C_K), the t-structure of Schneiders, the left heart LH(C_K) with the embedding I and the classical-part functor C, the equivalence D(C_K) ≅ D(LH(C_K)), the two facts on extensions and on degreewise strict exactness, the dual right-hearted version, and the definition of classical cohomology. (5) Tensor products: the projective and injective topologies, their coincidence over a spherically complete field, left exactness of (−) ⊗̂_K W with density of the image and surjectivity in the Fréchet case, the interchange with countable projective limits of Fréchet spaces and with regular inductive limits with injective nuclear transition maps, nuclear and compact maps, regular and acyclic inductive systems with Wengenroth's criterion (Proposition 2.2), and the derived functor ⊗̂^R_K with Lemma 2.3 (when ⊗̂ computes ⊗̂^R). (6) The integral theory: pro-discrete O_K-modules PD_K, the pseudocompact subcategory PC_K, the ind-completion Ind(PD_K) with its exactness properties, the completed tensor product of pro-discrete modules and its right exactness on PC_K, the rationalisation (−) ⊗ K with the counterexample to left exactness, its left derived functors with values in a pro-category, and Proposition 2.6 with Lemma 2.7 (a strict exact sequence of pro-discrete modules with torsion-free p-adically complete quotient splits, so rationalisation is undistorted on such complexes). Construct or identify the shared nonarchimedean Banach/Fréchet and compact-type foundations once; L0 consumes these in its function-space constructions but does not itself certify this general foundation. Supply it to L0 and the other consumers without a cycle.

independentReview.reason: Reject pending a shared-foundation design. LocallyAnalyticDistributions L0/L4 is a reasonable analytic parent, but it is itself a consumer of generic nonarchimedean convex/derived theory. Specify one common exact/derived carrier, its relation to existing abelian derived categories, and imports for all consumers; do not silently assume L0 supplies Banach/Fréchet foundations. Close the integral pro-discrete and rationalization proof contracts, all definition APIs and tests. E8 supplies no reason to strengthen Lemma 2.3.

routes.title: Locally analytic representations of p-adic reductive groups
routes.reason: This is the roadmap proposed by PAPER-DING-25 for admissible locally analytic representations, the Schneider–Teitelbaum distribution algebra and the Orlik–Strauch functors. This paper needs exactly two statements from it, and is a source for the second: that the two outer terms of its pro-étale exact sequence are duals of admissible locally analytic representations of finite length, the left-hand one by Orlik–Strauch (Remark 1.6), and that the locally analytic generalized Steinberg representation Sp^an_J(L) is a space of compact type containing Sp_J(L) as the subspace killed by the Lie algebra, topologically reducible with Jordan–Hölder constituents described by Orlik–Schraen (Remark 5.5). Joining that proposal rather than opening a third roadmap.
routes.brief: Add to the roadmap proposed by PAPER-DING-25 the locally analytic generalized Steinberg representations of GL_{d+1}(K): construct Sp^an_J(L) for L a finite extension of Q_p or a closed subfield of C, prove that it is of compact type with nuclear Fréchet dual, that Sp_J(L) is its subspace of vectors killed by the Lie algebra and hence closed, that dually Sp^an_J(L)^* surjects onto Sp_J(L)^* and contains Sp^cont_J(L)^* densely, and prove the Orlik–Schraen theorem describing the Jordan–Hölder constituents of the locally analytic Steinberg representation. Prove in addition the finiteness statement this paper quotes: for 1 ≤ r ≤ d the spaces Ω^{r−1}(H^d_C)/ker d and Sp_r(Q_p)^* are duals of admissible locally analytic representations of G of finite length, the first over C by Orlik–Strauch. The smooth and continuous Steinberg representations themselves belong to the Drinfeld symmetric spaces roadmap above, which is where they are constructed.
